chapters.title: Chapter 4: When Sustainability Fails: Default, Restructuring, and Contagion

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Sovereign Default: Sri Lanka 2022 and Zambia 2020

body.text: Every sovereign default looks inevitable in hindsight and completely avoidable a year before it happens. The anatomy is never one shock. It is a sequence of smaller failures that compound until a government simply cannot find the dollars.

children.text: The first three chapters built the tools to read sustainability and applied them to India, arriving at a genuinely reassuring baseline with a specific, well-defined tail risk. This chapter studies the other side of that coin: what actually happens when sustainability fails for real. This lesson takes apart two of the most recent, most thoroughly documented sovereign defaults, Sri Lanka in 2022 and Zambia in 2020, not for their outcomes alone but for their sequence: what built up quietly, what triggered the acute phase, and what the market was already saying before either government publicly admitted distress.
Sri Lanka: Anatomy of a Preventable Collapse

events.title: Easter Bombings Hit Tourism
events.description: Coordinated terrorist attacks devastate Sri Lanka's tourism sector, one of its largest sources of foreign currency, right before the pandemic would strike the same sector even harder.

events.title: Large, Ill-Timed Tax Cuts
events.description: A newly elected government enacts sweeping tax cuts, sharply reducing government revenue just before a global shock that would demand far more fiscal space, not less.

events.title: Covid-19 Collapses Foreign Exchange Earnings
events.description: Tourism revenue and remittances both fall sharply during the pandemic, draining the foreign currency Sri Lanka needed to service its heavily foreign-currency-denominated debt.

events.title: A Sudden Ban on Chemical Fertiliser Imports
events.description: The government abruptly mandates a shift to organic farming, banning chemical fertiliser imports. Agricultural output and export crops fall sharply, compounding the foreign exchange shortage rather than easing it.

events.title: Reserves Collapse
events.description: Usable foreign exchange reserves fall toward critically low levels, triggering severe fuel, food, and medicine shortages and mass public protests, known as the Aragalaya movement.

events.title: Sri Lanka Declares Default
events.description: The government announces a pre-emptive suspension of external debt payments, the first sovereign default in Sri Lanka's history.

events.title: President Rajapaksa Resigns
events.description: Amid continued mass protests, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa flees the country and resigns, a direct political consequence of the economic collapse.

events.title: The IMF Program Is Secured
events.description: Sri Lanka reaches a staff-level agreement with the IMF for an Extended Fund Facility of roughly $2.9 billion in September 2022, formally approved by the IMF's board in March 2023.

stats.label: Usable FX Reserves, April 2022
stats.context: Down from over $7.5 billion just a few years earlier

stats.label: ISB Share of External Debt
stats.context: International Sovereign Bonds were the single largest category of Sri Lanka's external debt

stats.label: GDP Contraction, 2022
stats.context: One of the sharpest peacetime contractions in the country's history

stats.label: Default Declared
stats.context: The first sovereign default in Sri Lanka's history

body.text: This is the same case flagged in Chapter 2 for its yield curve: Sri Lanka's USD bond curve inverted sharply well before the April 2022 declaration, and its CDS spreads had already priced in a near-certain default months earlier. The market signals this course has spent an entire chapter teaching you to read were visible long before the government's own public statements caught up.

children.text: Zambia: The First Test of the G20 Common Framework

events.title: A Borrowing Build-Up, Partly Opaque
events.description: Zambia borrows heavily through the 2010s, including Eurobonds and a significant share from Chinese state-linked lenders on non-Paris-Club terms, some of it not fully captured in official debt statistics, the same blind spot covered in Chapter 1.

events.title: Copper Price Volatility Bites
events.description: Zambia's economy remains heavily dependent on copper exports for foreign currency earnings; falling and volatile copper prices strain the country's ability to service its growing external debt.

events.title: Zambia Misses a Eurobond Coupon
events.description: Zambia fails to make a $42.5 million Eurobond coupon payment, becoming Africa's first pandemic-era sovereign default.

events.title: Zambia Requests the G20 Common Framework
events.description: Zambia becomes the first country to formally seek debt treatment under the G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments, launched only weeks earlier, with no precedent for how the process would actually work.

events.title: An IMF Program Provides an Anchor
events.description: Zambia secures a $1.3 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility, intended to anchor the restructuring negotiations, though actual debt relief agreements would still take considerable time to follow.

events.title: Official Creditors Reach an Agreement
events.description: Zambia's Official Creditor Committee, including China as the largest bilateral creditor, reaches an agreement in principle on roughly $6.3 billion of official bilateral debt, nearly three years after the original default.

events.title: Private Bondholders Follow
events.description: A separate agreement with Zambia's Eurobond holders follows, including new bonds carrying a haircut and value-recovery instruments tied to Zambia's future economic performance.

body.text: Nearly three years passed between Zambia's default and a completed official-creditor agreement, and longer still before private bondholders settled. Being the first country through a brand-new framework meant Zambia absorbed the cost of every unresolved question about how official creditors, especially a large non-Paris-Club lender, would actually coordinate with each other. The next lesson looks specifically at why the Common Framework moves this slowly.

children.text: What Both Cases Share, and Where They Differ

columns.label: Shared Features
points: Heavy reliance on foreign-currency borrowing that domestic reserves alone could not service once FX earnings fell
A single dominant export or earnings sector, tourism for Sri Lanka, copper for Zambia, whose disruption directly triggered the FX shortfall
Debt burdens that were, to different degrees, underappreciated before the crisis
An IMF program sought only after default, used as the anchor for the restructuring negotiations that followed

columns.label: What Set Them Apart
points: Sri Lanka's crisis was substantially self-inflicted through domestic policy, the 2019 tax cuts and the 2021 fertiliser ban, layered on top of external shocks
Zambia's case was the first-ever test of the G20 Common Framework, exposing how slow official-creditor coordination could be in practice
Sri Lanka additionally restructured part of its domestic rupee-denominated debt, a rare step most sovereign defaults do not include
China's role differed in emphasis: central and often the pacing item in Zambia's negotiations, more readily folded into the joint creditor process in Sri Lanka's

cells: Tourism (hit by the 2019 Easter bombings, then Covid-19)
Copper exports (exposed to commodity price swings)
2019 tax cuts and a 2021 sudden ban on chemical fertiliser imports
No comparable single domestic policy shock; a longer build-up of borrowing
Less about hidden debt, more about a rapid, visible fiscal and reserve deterioration
Opaque, non-Paris-Club borrowing made the true scale of external debt genuinely unclear at default
A pre-emptive suspension of external debt payments, announced 12 April 2022
A missed $42.5 million Eurobond coupon payment, 13 November 2020
IMF EFF (staff-level Sept 2022, board approval March 2023); included a rare domestic debt restructuring
First country under the G20 Common Framework; IMF ECF August 2022; Official Creditor Committee agreement mid-2023

children.text: The Common Sequence: From Stress to Declaration

Strip away the country-specific details and both cases follow a recognisable sequence. A structural vulnerability builds up quietly, a heavy reliance on one FX-earning sector, or debt whose true scale is not fully visible even to the government's own creditors. A shock, external or self-inflicted, hits revenue or reserves directly. Market signals, the inverted yield curves and widening CDS spreads covered in Chapter 2, start flashing well before the government publicly admits distress. Usable reserves fall toward a genuine floor, the point at which there simply is not enough foreign currency to meet a scheduled payment, forcing either a messy, disorderly default or a pre-emptive one. An IMF program is then sought, not to prevent the default at that late stage, but to serve as the anchor and financing-assurance mechanism creditors need before they will even begin restructuring talks. And the restructuring itself, covered in depth in the next lesson, then takes years, not months, to conclude.

body.title: Which Stage Is This Country In?
body.scenario: A frontier sovereign has seen its usable FX reserves fall by 60% over 18 months, driven by a collapse in its single largest export commodity's price. Its 5-year CDS spread has widened from 300 bps to 1,800 bps over the same period, and its short-dated USD bond yields now sit well above its 10-year bond yields. The government has not missed any payment yet and continues to describe its finances as 'fully manageable' in public statements.
body.prompt: Using the anatomy from this lesson, which stage is this country most likely in, and what would you expect to happen next if nothing changes?
body.modelAnswer: This sits squarely in the stage where market signals have already moved well ahead of any government acknowledgement of distress: the CDS spike and the inverted curve are the market pricing a high, near-term probability of default, exactly the pattern covered in Chapter 2, while the government's public messaging still describes the position as manageable, mirroring both Sri Lanka's and Zambia's governments in the months before their own defaults. If reserves continue falling toward a genuine floor with no policy response or external financing arranged, the most likely next steps, based on both case studies, are either a missed payment forcing a default declaration or a pre-emptive suspension of payments, followed by an IMF program sought as the anchor for what would likely be a multi-year restructuring process.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Zambia's 2020 default was significant for a specific institutional reason beyond the default itself. What made it notable?
options: It was the first sovereign default in African history
It was the first country to seek debt treatment under the newly created G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments, testing a mechanism that had never been used before
It was the first default where the IMF refused to provide any financing at all
It was resolved within three months of the missed payment, the fastest sovereign restructuring on record
body.explanation: Zambia's November 2020 default made it the first country to request debt treatment under the G20 Common Framework, launched just weeks earlier. Its slow, multi-year negotiation, roughly three years from default to an Official Creditor Committee agreement, became a widely cited early test of how the framework actually performs in practice, a theme the next lesson explores in depth.

children.text: A Field Checklist for Spotting a Default Building

body.title: Before You Assume a Sovereign Won't Default
steps: Check usable FX reserves specifically, not gross reserves, and their trend over the past 12 to 18 months, not just the latest snapshot
Identify the single largest FX-earning sector and its recent price or volume trend; tourism, a single export commodity, or remittances often carry outsized weight
Check the currency composition of upcoming debt maturities over the next 12 to 24 months, not just the total debt stock
Cross-check the bond yield curve shape and CDS spread trend from Chapter 2, since both cases showed the market moving well ahead of any government acknowledgement
Look specifically for opaque or non-standard borrowing, non-Paris-Club bilateral loans or off-budget items, that could be larger than officially disclosed, as in Zambia's case
Watch for abrupt, self-inflicted policy shocks, a sudden tax cut or an unexplained ban on a key input, that can compound an external shock rather than cushion it, as in Sri Lanka's case

body.text: This lesson describes the sequence of events in Sri Lanka's and Zambia's sovereign defaults for educational purposes, based on public reporting. It is not investment advice, and figures, dates, and negotiation details are approximate; always verify against official IMF, government, and creditor-committee statements for the current status of any ongoing restructuring.

points: Sri Lanka's 2022 default followed a sequence of largely self-inflicted shocks, the 2019 tax cuts and 2021 fertiliser ban, compounding external shocks like Covid-19's hit to tourism, ending in a pre-emptive default and, unusually, a domestic debt restructuring

Zambia's 2020 default made it the first test case for the G20 Common Framework, and the roughly three-year gap to an official-creditor agreement exposed how slow that framework's coordination can be in practice

Both cases show bond yields and CDS spreads (Chapter 2) moving well ahead of any government acknowledgement of distress, reinforcing that market signals are a leading, not lagging, indicator in real defaults

A generalisable anatomy emerges: a quiet structural vulnerability, an external or self-inflicted shock, market signals flashing early, reserves hitting a genuine floor, an IMF program sought as an anchor, and a multi-year restructuring that follows
The next lesson goes inside that restructuring process itself, the mechanics of haircuts, reprofiling, and the G20 Common Framework that both Sri Lanka and Zambia had to navigate
